reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents a front-running and sandwich-trading bot as an easy income mechanism and links its claimed profits to transactions placed around another user's transaction. It instructs viewers to deploy and fund the contract with BNB, says larger funding can produce more profit, and claims that most profits are automatically returned to the viewer's wallet. Reported weekly returns and profitability claims reinforce the promotional financial context, although it includes a non-guarantee disclaimer and does not independently verify the bot, its code, or the claimed outcomes.

the victim transaction gets sandwiched between ours and we make a small
profit off the slippage difference in the transaction

the more the better because the larger the more you put in the larger the transaction you'll be able to front run and the more profit you'll be able to make

opening.argument: Judge the income claims alongside the warnings that qualify them. The description calls cryptocurrency a high-risk investment, says trading can result in loss, and expressly disclaims any guaranteed outcome. The speaker also warns that the bot could encounter a honeypot and says participation is at the viewer's own risk. Those are material qualifications to the reported returns, not a promise that funding the contract will reliably produce income.

citations.quote: Cryptocurrency is HIGHLY volatile and a very high-risk investment. Trading cryptocurrencies poses considerable risk of loss.
The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.
It could be a honeypot or some kind of shitcoin contract, who knows
however it's at your own risk

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited funding instruction establishes what the proposed bot requires, not that viewers are promised a return. Likewise, the description of placing transactions around another user's trade explains the proposed trading mechanism; it does not establish that the claimed profits occurred or were guaranteed. The prosecution's reading leaves out the explicit risk-of-loss warning and non-guarantee that qualify the pitch.

Trading cryptocurrencies poses considerable risk of loss. The speaker does not guarantee any particular outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A non-guarantee does not undo the video's concrete invitation to fund a bot for returns. The speaker calls the proposed trading income easy and passive, says more funding can mean more profit, and claims the contract automatically sends most profits back to the viewer's wallet. The warnings qualify those claims but do not change the funded-contract income pitch.

opening.argument: This is principally a walkthrough of a Solidity workflow. The speaker introduces a step-by-step build, creates a contract file in Remix, then explains compiling and deploying it. They also tell viewers to inspect the contract themselves and express distrust of opaque executable downloads. Showing how a proposed bot is configured and run, even while discussing potential earnings, is consistent with a technical demonstration; the walkthrough itself does not independently establish that its performance claims are true.

This will be our contract. You can name it whatever you like however I'm going to name mine EVM frontrunner
we are going to compile our contract in remix
you guys can scan through this yourself
I personally, don't trust anything unless it's open source

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution correctly identifies discussion of sandwich trading, but explaining a mechanism is not, by itself, proof of a fraudulent solicitation. The cited deployment and funding steps occur within the described contract walkthrough. Nor do claims about possible profit verify that the demonstrated code delivers it; the speaker explicitly invites viewers to inspect the contract.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial format does not make the funding step incidental. After deployment, the speaker directs viewers to fund the contract, says the bot will return profits to their wallets, and reports a profitable return during the demonstration. Code inspection is suggested, but the provided material does not verify that the linked contract performs as claimed.

citations.quote: The next step in the process is we're going to need to fund our contract with BNB
it will automatically send 90% of the profits that are made from the contracts that it sniffs directly back to your wallet address
as you can see here we've already gotten a return back from our contracts look at that 0.24. Very profitable guys.

opening.argument: The material points viewers to software and a trading tool, but it does not establish that they are paying the creator for access or sending funds to a stated creator-controlled account. The speaker describes copying contract code into Remix and says the contract must be funded to trade; those steps are also compatible with a user operating their own tool. The description offers a second bot while saying viewers may choose either. Without evidence of who controls the deployed contract or receives its funds, the funding instruction alone cannot settle that this is a scheme to take viewers' deposits.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's strongest point is the instruction to fund a contract in pursuit of profit. But its citations do not identify the deployed contract's controller, show a payment to the creator, or verify what happens to deposited BNB. The statement that larger trades could make more profit is a claim about trade size, not evidence of a guaranteed payout or a disclosed fee to the speaker.

citations.quote: we're going to need to fund our contract with BNB, to be able to snipe liquidity pools
the more you put in the larger the transaction you'll be able to front run and the more profit you'll be able to make

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of proof about who controls the contract is not evidence that funding it is safe. The video directs viewers to use linked contract code, fund the deployed contract with BNB, and expect automatically returned profits. Those are the operative steps of the promoted income mechanism even without a demonstrated creator payment or a guaranteed-return statement.
